title: The hypertrophy series: absolute vs relative intensity
summary: NH defines absolute intensity as your fresh, warmed-up ability to move weight, which changes only slowly with strength progress, and relative intensity as the declining capacity during a session. Strength work uses absolute intensity at the start, while the rest happens in relative intensity windows. Junk volume is sets that fall outside a relevant window measured against absolute intensity, not relative.
claims: Absolute intensity is your ability to move weight in a fresh, warmed-up state: the maximum you can exert before any fatigue
You are not at absolute intensity until warmed up, because muscles are not yet filled with blood and joints not flooded with synovial fluid
Absolute intensity changes very slowly, driven only by strength progression; relative intensity is the value that moves within a session
Strength work opens the session because that is when absolute intensity is fully available and the most tonnage can be moved
If you could keep only one part of the training session, it would be the strength work
Most tonnage progress comes from the work that follows strength work, in relative intensity windows
End the session when you can no longer return to a baseline that is relevant to your absolute intensity
If you squat 400 lb and can no longer do 260 for 4-5 reps, the muscle is spent and you are in irrelevant intensity windows
Basing workloads only on relative intensity would keep you training for hours because relative intensity keeps dropping with you
There is an irreducible baseline: a load you can always move however tired you are, like 135 for someone with a 300 lb squat, and training with it is pointless
NH programs with percentages rather than RPE, but both work for hypertrophy
You do not need to test a 1RM; base percentages on a 4RM or 6RM, since 1RM strength does not strictly correlate with rep strength
NH does not know his one-rep max and never goes below 4 reps on squats
Using absolute and relative intensity correctly gives sessions just long enough to progress without excess fatigue or wasted time
Junk volume is sets done outside a window of relevance compared to absolute intensity, not relative intensity
Once you know your absolute intensity it stays put; track how relative intensity evolves from lift to lift to know what challenges the muscle
